corrections.was: A code box shows one clip, named attack fast. An Animation resource is stored animation data, a length plus tracks of keys, and nothing else. This one is zero point four five seconds long, with a rotation track and a method track among its four. It is data, not behaviour, so nothing moves until a player plays it. For example, a spinning coin in your game could be a single Animation resource with one rotation track, saved in the coin's scene file.
corrections.now: A code box shows one clip, named attack fast. An Animation resource is stored animation data, a length plus tracks of keys. This one is zero point four five seconds long, with a rotation track and a method track among its four. It is data, not behaviour, so nothing moves until a player plays it. For example, a spinning coin in your game could be a single Animation resource with one rotation track, saved in the coin's scene file.
corrections.why: 'and nothing else' overclaims: the code box on screen also shows step = 0.05, and Chapter 10 keeps loop_mode on the Animation too; the slide says only 'a length plus tracks of keys'.

corrections.was: Callback modes set when animation updates, idle or physics, and when method keys run, deferred or immediate. Here a key at zero point one zero seconds, at one hundred twenty frames per second, falls on frame twelve on paper. Play leaves the first frame at zero, and a deferred call waits for the frame to end, so on the Walker sword it was observed on frame fourteen. For example, a test asserting that your sword's method key fires on frame twelve would fail.
corrections.now: Callback modes set when animation updates, idle or physics, and when method keys run, deferred or immediate. Here a key at zero point one zero seconds, at one hundred twenty frames per second, falls on frame twelve on paper. Play leaves the playhead at zero on the first frame, and a deferred call waits for the frame to end, so on the Walker sword it was observed on frame fourteen. For example, a test asserting that your sword's method key fires on frame twelve would fail.
corrections.why: It is the playhead that stays at 0.0 on the first frame after play(), per the slide ('+1 play() leaves the playhead at 0.0 on the first frame') and Chapter 10 'Starting'; 'leaves the first frame at zero' reads as frame numbering.

corrections.was: Now the hand chases a moving target. Inverse kinematics, or IK, means you choose the target, and the solver computes the joint angles that reach it. For two bones the law of cosines solves it. In this made-up arm the target is one hundred ninety-one from the shoulder, out of a reach of two hundred eighty, and the elbow bends to eighty-six degrees. For example, in the Walker IK build the mouse moves a target, and the robot's arms are solved to reach it.
corrections.now: Now the hand chases a moving target. Inverse kinematics, or IK, means you choose the target, and the solver computes the joint angles that reach it. For two bones the law of cosines solves it. In this made-up arm the target is one hundred ninety-one from the shoulder, out of a reach of two hundred eighty, and the angle at the elbow is eighty-six degrees. For example, in the Walker IK build the mouse moves a target, and the robot's arms are solved to reach it.
corrections.why: 86 degrees is the interior elbow angle (the deck's twoBone uses acos of the law of cosines; 150 and 130 at 191 gives 85.7), while two beats earlier the film measures the forearm as a bend from a straight rest pose of 0, so 'bends to 86' would teach the opposite reading.

corrections.was: Four rows of frame ticks, from a simulated run. A Fixed frame rate, set with the fixed fps flag and a number, makes every frame advance game time by exactly one over that number, in seconds. Pinned, the first frame past zero point one seconds is frame twelve every time. Unpinned, it drifts between twelve and thirteen. For example, the sword timing test written for Walker passed twenty of twenty pinned, and failed seven, nine and nine checks without the flag.
corrections.now: Four rows of frame ticks, from a simulated run. A Fixed frame rate, set with the fixed fps flag and a number, makes every frame advance game time by exactly one over that number, in seconds. Pinned, the first frame at or past zero point one seconds is frame twelve every time. Unpinned, it drifts between twelve and thirteen. For example, the sword timing test written for Walker passed twenty of twenty pinned, and failed seven, nine and nine checks without the flag.
corrections.why: The slide's heading is 'FIRST FRAME AT OR PAST 0.10 S'; at 120 fps frame 12 lands exactly on 0.1 s, so it is not past it.

corrections.was: Make the arm reach the target becomes, two-bone IK from shoulder to hand, with a pole target above the elbow. At a reach of one hundred the elbow angle is forty-one degrees, and at two hundred seventy it is one hundred forty-nine. A farther target means a straighter elbow.
corrections.now: Make the arm reach the target becomes, two-bone IK from shoulder to hand, with a pole target above the elbow. At a target distance of one hundred the elbow angle is forty-one degrees, and at two hundred seventy it is one hundred forty-nine. A farther target means a straighter elbow.
corrections.why: Two beats on IK use 'reach' for two things: slide 8 says reach 280 is the arm's full length, while here the slide's 'reach 100' is the distance to the target; saying 'target distance' keeps the term consistent.

unresolved: slide 3 step 4: narration says nearest 'takes the value of the closest key', which matches the deck's own vNear code, but the slide caption says 'nearest holds' and neither Chapter 10 nor the glossary says whether Godot's nearest picks the closest or the previous key; at 0.06 s both give -80, so the beat was left.

slide 11 step 2: narration says 'only a loop needs its first and last values to match'; mechanically true (ping-pong reverses, so it never jumps), but Chapter 10's loop-seam test pairs matching values with loop_mode LOOP_LINEAR or LOOP_PINGPONG without separating them; left as is.
